blocks.x: If you’ve ever stared at your computer screen on a Thursday afternoon and wished the weekend would just start already, a wave of new legislation could eventually make that a reality.

A renewed push to reduce the standard American workweek from 40 hours to 32 hours—without a loss in pay—is making the rounds at both the state and federal levels. Between active bills in the New York State Assembly and a fresh push in Congress earlier this month, the traditional five-day grind is facing its biggest challenge in nearly a century.
So, what exactly would these laws do—and is New York really about to adopt a permanent three-day weekend? Here’s what you need to know.
What is the 4-day workweek proposal?

The core idea stems from the global 4 Day Week Campaign, an advocacy group established in 2019 that pushes for the “100-80-100 model.” The idea is simple: workers receive 100% of their pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for maintaining 100% productivity.
Lawmakers are now trying to code this into law.
On September 8, 2026, Senator Bernie Sanders and California Representative Mark Takano reintroduced the Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act to Congress.
The legislation would federally redefine the standard workweek, reducing it from 40 hours to 32 hours. The goal is to build a world where Americans “work to live, rather than live to work.”

Unsplash / Israel Andrade
The main details
If the federal and state pushes are successful, it would mean massive changes for how New Yorkers clock in. Here’s what the legislation proposes:

A gradual phase-in: According to the federal legislation, the standard workweek wouldn’t drop to 32 hours overnight. It would decrease gradually over four years, reducing work hours by two hours each year until reaching the 32-hour mark
Overtime kicks in earlier: Under the federal bill, non-exempt employees would earn time-and-a-half pay for any hours worked beyond the new 32-hour limit

New York state has its own bills: In February 2025, Assembly Bill A5454 (focusing on private employees) and Assembly Bill A5423 (focusing on state employees) were introduced in Albany, hoping to bring New York specifically one step closer to a mandated 4-day week
NYC has already been testing the waters
While a permanent 32-hour week hasn’t been codified yet, New York City has already experimented with altering the traditional five-day schedule.

In January 2024, former Mayor Eric Adams introduced a compressed workweek pilot for members of the city’s largest public employee union, District Council 37 (DC 37), whose jobs could not be performed remotely.
Under this pilot, eligible employees could work a four-day week—or alternate between four- and five-day weeks—by working longer hours on their on-days to complete the traditional 40-hour requirement.
City and union leadership noted that the alternative schedules boosted employee morale, aided in staff retention, and maintained public service efficiency.

Unsplash / Benny Rotlevy
Why is this happening?
The 40-hour workweek was established into law nearly 90 years ago, and lawmakers argue that times have fundamentally changed.

In a press release for the September 2026 push, lawmakers pointed out that cell phones, the internet, and artificial intelligence (AI) have drastically increased worker productivity, but the financial benefits have largely bypassed the working class.
Furthermore, global pilots of the 4-day workweek have shown incredibly promising results. Participating businesses and governments have reported:
Climbing productivity and lower operational costs
Better work-life balance and heightened morale for workers
Fewer sick days and lower childcare expenses for families
Positive environmental impacts due to reduced commuting
People continue to work longer hours while their pay remains stagnant. We cannot continue to accept this as our reality. – Takano
So, is New York actually switching to a 4-day workweek?
Not yet.

While the conversation is louder than ever, both the federal Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act and New York’s Assembly bills (A5454 and A5423) are still just proposals. The New York bills currently remain active in their respective legislative committees for the 2025–2026 session, and the federal bill faces a long battle in Congress.
None of these have been passed into law or gone into effect.

So for now, New Yorkers will have to keep hustling like we do best. But with lawmakers repeatedly bringing the issue to the table, the dream of a standard three-day weekend may just be getting closer to reality.
